items.readable_text:
Content:
Given a matrix [MATH: A,] an eigenvector of [MATH: A] is a non-zero vector [MATH: \mathbf{v}] such that
[MATH: A \mathbf{v} = \lambda \mathbf{v}]
for some scalar [MATH: \lambda \in \mathbb{R}.] The scalar [MATH: \lambda] is called the eigenvalue corresponding to the eigenvector [MATH: \mathbf{v}.]

Content:
For example, consider the matrix
[MATH: [2|2; 2|− 1]]
and the vector [MATH: [1; − 2]] Computing the product [MATH: A \cdot \mathbf{v},] we get
[MATH: Av|= [2|2; 2|− 1] ⋅ [1; − 2]; = [− 2; 4]; = (− 2) ⋅ [1; − 2]; = − 2v.]

Content:
We've discovered that [MATH: A {\color{blue}\mathbf{v}} = {\color{red}-2} {\color{blue}\mathbf{v}}.] Therefore,

Content:
- the vector [MATH: [1; − 2]] is an eigenvector of [MATH: A,] and
- the scalar [MATH: \color{red}\lambda=-2] is the eigenvalue corresponding to the eigenvector [MATH: {\color{blue}\mathbf{v}}.]

Content:
Caution: Remember that an eigenvector must be a non-zero vector. This is very important.

Eigenvectors and eigenvalues can be interpreted geometrically.

Content:
First, recall that if the matrix [MATH: A] is the standard matrix of some linear transformation [MATH: \mathbf A,] then the product [MATH: A\mathbf x] gives the image of [MATH: \mathbf x] under the action of [MATH: \mathbf A.] Under the action of [MATH: \mathbf A,] the image of [MATH: \mathbf x] can appear quite different to the original vector [MATH: \mathbf x.]

Content:
In other words, when the matrix [MATH: A] is applied to an eigenvector [MATH: \mathbf{v},] the image of [MATH: \mathbf v] is a scaled version of the original vector [MATH: \mathbf v], and the scale factor is [MATH: \lambda.]

In general, when we apply a matrix [MATH: A] to an eigenvector [MATH: \mathbf{v},] the resulting vector [MATH: A\mathbf{v}=\lambda\mathbf{v}] always lies on the same line as [MATH: \mathbf{v}.]

sections.normalized_html: An eigenvector of [MATH: 2|1; 1|2] corresponding to an eigenvalue [MATH: \lambda=6c] is [MATH: 1; 2c] Determine the value of [MATH: c.]
sections.readable_text: An eigenvector of [MATH: 2|1; 1|2] corresponding to an eigenvalue [MATH: \lambda=6c] is [MATH: 1; 2c] Determine the value of [MATH: c.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Remember that the eigenvectors of [MATH: A] are the non-zero vectors [MATH: \mathbf{v}] such that [MATH: A\mathbf{v}=\lambda \mathbf{v}.] So, we have

[MATH: Av|= λv; [2|1; 1|2][1; 2c]|= 6c[1; 2c]; [2 + 2c; 1 + 4c]|= [6c; 12c^{2}].]

This gives us the following system of linear equations:

[MATH: {2 + 2c = 6c; 1 + 4c = 12c^{2}]

Solving for [MATH: c] in the first equation, we get [MATH: 2+2c=6c \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad c = \dfrac{1}{2}.]

Now, substituting [MATH: c=\dfrac{1}{2}] into the second equation, we get [MATH: 1 + 4c|= 12c^{2}; 1 + 4 ⋅ (1)/(2)|= 12((1)/(2))^{2}; 3|= 3,] which is a true statement.

Therefore, the solutions of the system is [MATH: c=\dfrac{1}{2}].

items.title: Identifying True Statements About Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors

sections.normalized_html:
Which of the following statements are true?

  1. [MATH: [1; 4]] is an eigenvector of [MATH: [2|0; 4|1]] that corresponds to the eigenvalue [MATH: 2.]

  2. [MATH: [0; 0]] is an eigenvector of [MATH: [1|1; 1|1]] that corresponds to the eigenvalue [MATH: 0.]

  3. If [MATH: \mathbf{v}] is an eigenvector of a matrix [MATH: A] corresponding to the eigenvalue [MATH: \lambda = 5,] then [MATH: 2\mathbf{v}] is also an eigenvector of [MATH: A] corresponding to [MATH: \lambda = 5.]
sections.readable_text:
Which of the following statements are true?

1. [MATH: [1; 4]] is an eigenvector of [MATH: [2|0; 4|1]] that corresponds to the eigenvalue [MATH: 2.]
2. [MATH: [0; 0]] is an eigenvector of [MATH: [1|1; 1|1]] that corresponds to the eigenvalue [MATH: 0.]
3. If [MATH: \mathbf{v}] is an eigenvector of a matrix [MATH: A] corresponding to the eigenvalue [MATH: \lambda = 5,] then [MATH: 2\mathbf{v}] is also an eigenvector of [MATH: A] corresponding to [MATH: \lambda = 5.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Remember that the eigenvectors of [MATH: A] are the non-zero vectors [MATH: \mathbf{v}] such that [MATH: A\mathbf{v}=\lambda \mathbf{v}.] With that in mind, let's examine the statements one by one.

  • Statement I is true. We have [MATH: Av|= [2|0; 4|1][1; 4]; = [2; 8]; = 2 ⋅ [1; 4]; = 2v.] Since [MATH: A\mathbf{v}=2 \mathbf{v},] we conclude that [MATH: \mathbf{v}] is an eigenvector of [MATH: A] and the corresponding eigenvalue is [MATH: \lambda=2.]

  • Statement II is false. An eigenvector must be a non-zero vector.

  • Statement III is true. We have [MATH: A(2v) = 2Av = 2(5v) = 5(2v).] Since, [MATH: A(2\mathbf{v})=5( 2 \mathbf{v} ),] and [MATH: 2 \mathbf{v} \neq \mathbf{0},] this implies that [MATH: 2 \mathbf{v}] is an eigenvector of [MATH: A] and the corresponding eigenvalue is [MATH: \lambda = 5.]

Therefore, the correct answer is, "I and III only."

Note: Statement III is true in the general case, too. In general, any non-zero multiple of an eigenvector is again an eigenvector, and the corresponding eigenvalue is the same.

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Given a matrix [MATH: A,] an eigenvector of [MATH: A] is a non-zero vector [MATH: \mathbf{v}] such that
[MATH: A \mathbf{v} = \lambda \mathbf{v}]
for some scalar [MATH: \lambda \in \mathbb{R}.] The scalar [MATH: \lambda] is called the eigenvalue corresponding to the eigenvector [MATH: \mathbf{v}.]

Content:
For example, consider the matrix
[MATH: [2|2; 2|− 1]]
and the vector [MATH: [1; − 2]] Computing the product [MATH: A \cdot \mathbf{v},] we get
[MATH: Av|= [2|2; 2|− 1] ⋅ [1; − 2]; = [− 2; 4]; = (− 2) ⋅ [1; − 2]; = − 2v.]

Content:
We've discovered that [MATH: A {\color{blue}\mathbf{v}} = {\color{red}-2} {\color{blue}\mathbf{v}}.] Therefore,

Content:
- the vector [MATH: [1; − 2]] is an eigenvector of [MATH: A,] and
- the scalar [MATH: \color{red}\lambda=-2] is the eigenvalue corresponding to the eigenvector [MATH: {\color{blue}\mathbf{v}}.]

Content:
Caution: Remember that an eigenvector must be a non-zero vector. This is very important.

---

Item 2 — Example: Finding the Eigenvalue that Corresponds to a Given Eigenvector

Example Prompt:
Determine if [MATH: 1; 1] is an eigenvector of the matrix [MATH: 1|3; 3|1] If so, then what is the corresponding eigenvalue?

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The eigenvectors of [MATH: A] are the non-zero vectors [MATH: \mathbf{v}] such that [MATH: A\mathbf{v}=\lambda \mathbf{v}.] We have
[MATH: Av|= [1|3; 3|1][1; 1]; = [4; 4]; = 4 ⋅ [1; 1]; = 4v.]

Since [MATH: A\mathbf{v}=4 \mathbf{v},] we conclude that [MATH: \mathbf{v}] is an eigenvector of [MATH: A] and the corresponding eigenvalue is [MATH: \lambda=4.]

Item 5 — Tutorial: The Geometric Interpretation of Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors

Content:
Eigenvectors and eigenvalues can be interpreted geometrically.

Content:
First, recall that if the matrix [MATH: A] is the standard matrix of some linear transformation [MATH: \mathbf A,] then the product [MATH: A\mathbf x] gives the image of [MATH: \mathbf x] under the action of [MATH: \mathbf A.] Under the action of [MATH: \mathbf A,] the image of [MATH: \mathbf x] can appear quite different to the original vector [MATH: \mathbf x.]

Content:
However, for an eigenvector [MATH: \mathbf v] with corresponding eigenvalue [MATH: \lambda,] we get

Content:
[MATH: A\mathbf v = \lambda \mathbf v.]

Content:
In other words, when the matrix [MATH: A] is applied to an eigenvector [MATH: \mathbf{v},] the image of [MATH: \mathbf v] is a scaled version of the original vector [MATH: \mathbf v], and the scale factor is [MATH: \lambda.]

Content:
To demonstrate, consider once again the following matrix:

Content:
[MATH: [2|2; 2|− 1]]

Content:
We've already seen that [MATH: A] has an eigenvector [MATH: [1; − 2]] with corresponding eigenvalue [MATH: {\color{black}\lambda=-2}.] So we have

Content:
[MATH: [− 2; 4]]

Content:
Plotting the vector [MATH: \mathbf v] and its image [MATH: -2\mathbf v] in the plane, we get the following picture.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/9d8976848db07d0cdf8392b21f15e54d]

Content:
In general, when we apply a matrix [MATH: A] to an eigenvector [MATH: \mathbf{v},] the resulting vector [MATH: A\mathbf{v}=\lambda\mathbf{v}] always lies on the same line as [MATH: \mathbf{v}.]

Content:
If [MATH: |\lambda| > 1,] then the matrix stretches the vector. For [MATH: |\lambda| < 1,] the matrix compresses the vector. In addition, a negative eigenvalue [MATH: \lambda < 0] means that [MATH: \mathbf v] is flipped in the opposite direction as well as scaled.

Item 9 — Example: Determining the Value of an Unknown Given an Eigenvalue and Eigenvector of a Matrix

Example Prompt:
An eigenvector of [MATH: 2|1; 1|2] corresponding to an eigenvalue [MATH: \lambda=6c] is [MATH: 1; 2c] Determine the value of [MATH: c.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Remember that the eigenvectors of [MATH: A] are the non-zero vectors [MATH: \mathbf{v}] such that [MATH: A\mathbf{v}=\lambda \mathbf{v}.] So, we have

[MATH: Av|= λv; [2|1; 1|2][1; 2c]|= 6c[1; 2c]; [2 + 2c; 1 + 4c]|= [6c; 12c^{2}].]

This gives us the following system of linear equations:

[MATH: {2 + 2c = 6c; 1 + 4c = 12c^{2}]

Solving for [MATH: c] in the first equation, we get
[MATH: 2+2c=6c \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad c = \dfrac{1}{2}.]

Now, substituting [MATH: c=\dfrac{1}{2}] into the second equation, we get
[MATH: 1 + 4c|= 12c^{2}; 1 + 4 ⋅ (1)/(2)|= 12((1)/(2))^{2}; 3|= 3,]
which is a true statement.

Therefore, the solutions of the system is [MATH: c=\dfrac{1}{2}].
